name: PT Astra Agro Lestari Tbk

frontmatter.title: Astra Agro Lestari: a cash-rich planter priced for a permanent downcycle
frontmatter.summary: Astra Agro Lestari is a vertically integrated Indonesian palm producer with a third of its market value in cash, no bank debt and a cash cost that moves with the fruit price. The market pays a multiple a terminal decline would justify for a business earning a mid-teens EBITDA margin. We rate BUY: even the bear case, with CPO a fifth below the deck, is worth more than the share price.
thesis: The market pays 3.0x enterprise value to EBITDA and 7.9x earnings for a planter that is debt-free, holds IDR5,792.2bn of cash and earned a nine-month EBITDA margin above the 16.1% we model for the full year; our DCF at the sector deck is worth Rp19,996, a 119.2% total return [S0, S3].

The Yahoo data pack misstates the P&L: its depreciation line of IDR167.5bn is the general-and-administrative charge alone, so the pack's EBIT and EBITDA are wrong; total FY2025 depreciation and amortisation is IDR1,462.9bn and EBITDA is IDR3,879.9bn, a 13.5% margin [S4, F9, F34].

Cost is price-linked, not fixed: raw materials and processing were IDR18,318.7bn in FY2025, most of the cost of revenue, so the cash-cost ratio has sat between four-fifths and five-sixths of revenue for three years [S4, F27].

The near-term swings are policy and weather, not the cycle: the November export-charge schedule, the B50 biodiesel mandate and a dry-weather hit to FFB yields into 2027 [S7, S6], while the planned relaxation of the export-proceeds conversion cap eases cash management but changes no revenue, cost or tax line [S8, S9].

Governance is clean but concentrated: Astra International owns most of the register, the related-party share of sales fell from 20 percent to 14 percent, and the dividend is paid in cash with no bank debt [S2, S3].

catalysts.event: Finance ministry regulation implementing the fourth revision to Government Regulation 36/2023, lifting the ceiling on conversion of natural-resource export proceeds into rupiah to the full amount
Trade ministry monthly schedule for the combined CPO export duty and levy
FY2026 audited results and the final dividend declaration; the interim was already paid in October 2026
Annual general meeting and the 2026 sustainability report
Evidence on the 2026-27 dry-weather impact on FFB yields and the replanting programme
Quarterly LK and the company's operational update on FFB processed and extraction rates

blocks.text: This revision repairs the fact base, removes a dividend double count and withdraws two unsupported claims. Three inputs changed: the realised-price ratio is held at the FY2025 level of 0.88 rather than lifted on the November export-charge schedule, which the source calls potential and resets monthly [S7, F28]; the October interim now sits inside the twelve-month dividend denominator rather than being deducted twice [S3, F33]; and the payout is anchored on the last actual of 59.9%, worth about sixty rupiah [S2, S4]. The rest is a peer re-read: median EV/EBITDA fell about a twelfth and median P/B a fiftieth, while no analyst cash-flow input changed [S0]. The lower target is not a view change.

We rate Astra Agro Lestari BUY with a twelve-month target of Rp19,996 against Rp9,450, a total return of 119.2% including the dividend [S0]. Astra International controls the register and the float is thin, so a debt-free estate business holding IDR5,792.2bn of cash changes hands at 3.0x enterprise value to EBITDA and 7.9x earnings [S2, S3]. The target is not a palm-oil spike: it is what the sector deck's own CPO path produces once cash cost is treated as the price-linked input the accounts show it to be [S4].

The most striking number is the bear case. With CPO a fifth below the deck, volume a tenth lower and unit cost giving ground, the bear value is Rp13,000, still above the Rp9,450 market price [S0, S7]. The earlier reverse-DCF claim, which rested on a corrupted engine field, is withdrawn.

The marker glides from US$1,135 in FY2026E to US$1,240 in FY2027E against a spot of US$1,180, so the forecast is not an extrapolation of the 2026 weather premium [S0, S7]; cost is roughly four-fifths price-linked, so a lower CPO price does not restore the margin as a fixed-cost miner would [S4, F27]; and capital allocation is a Rp720 twelve-month dividend with no bank debt, replanting paid from cash [S2, S3].

The data pack misstates depreciation, operating cost and dividend per share. We restate all three from the audited accounts and the interim filing — FY2025 depreciation and amortisation IDR1,462.9bn not IDR167.5bn, selling and administrative expense IDR2,214.4bn not the pack's lower line [S4, S3, F5, F9].

Astra Agro Lestari owns nucleus estates and processes its own, plasma and third-party fruit into crude palm oil, palm kernel and derivatives through thirty-two mills, fourteen crushers and three refineries [S2]. The estate is 280,325 hectares, about ninety-three percent mature, and the company processed 6,231 thousand tonnes of fruit in FY2025 [S2, F4, F12].

One product dominates. In the first nine months of FY2026 crude palm oil and derivatives produced IDR20,871.4bn of IDR23,714.3bn net revenue, kernel the bulk of the balance [S3, F17, F18]. Volume is what the company controls: 1,760 thousand tonnes of crude palm oil and derivatives sold in FY2025, up from 1,550 thousand, plus 247 thousand tonnes of kernel, with 36 percent exported, so the realised price carries the export wedge [S2, F1, F13, F14].

The tree is the asset and the age profile is the strategic problem. Average tree age is 16.70 years, 184,635 hectares — about two-thirds of the estate — are over fifteen years old, and the productive four-to-fifteen-year cohort has fallen to 76,292 hectares from a far larger base in 2021 [S2, F37, F38, F39]. Replanting of 5,080 hectares a year is a rotation beyond fifty years against a twenty-to-twenty-five-year cycle, and the FY2026 fruit target of 3.8 Mt is flat to lower against FY2025's 3,821.56 thousand tonnes [S2, F25, F20, F36]. Strategy is yield renewal on a fixed land bank, with part of the downstream margin earned through subsidiaries and a half-owned associate [S2].

Astra International controls the great majority of the register and the free float is 20.3% [S2, S0]. Sales to affiliates were 14 percent of nine-month revenue against 20 percent a year earlier, a shrinking channel [S3, F19, F41].

Indonesia is the world's largest palm producer and exporter, and the industry turns on a slow biological supply response against a policy-managed demand base [S2]. A tree planted today yields nothing for years and peaks a decade later, so the 2026 crop was set by planting decisions of the previous decade and by weather [S2].

Weather moves the near term both ways. The 2026 recovery has been partly attributed to conditions easing after an earlier weather hit, and the deck assumes a 2026-27 El Nino pulls the 2027 crop down again before supply normalises, which is why the price path peaks in FY2027E and then fades [S6, S0].

Demand is where the structural change sits. Indonesia moved to a fifty percent biodiesel blend in July 2026, converting a discretionary food and oleochemical market into a policy-anchored base load and supporting the deck's long-run marker of US$1,150, above the realised average of the past three years [S7, S0]. The same policy tightens the exportable surplus, so fiscal and industrial interests pull against each other [S7].

Policy sets the wedge between benchmark and realisation. Exports carry a duty and levy struck off a periodic reference price; the November-2026 schedule cuts the combined charge to US$246 a tonne, about a fifth below the prior month [S7, F28]. We do not carry that cut: the source calls it potential and it resets monthly, so the realised ratio stays at FY2025's 0.88 [S7, S4]. The domestic reference price was 14,943 a kilogram in October 2026 and the Rotterdam benchmark was US$1,222 a tonne in FY2025, so the calibrated ratio captures all three prices [S7, S2, F15, S4]. The export-proceeds relaxation changes the convertibility of recognised cash, not its size, and with IDR5,792.2bn of cash and no bank debt the company is not liquidity-constrained [S9, S8, F22].

Competition is fragmented upstream and concentrated downstream: many growers and few buyers of fruit in any catchment, so the mill with a radius holds a local advantage and the grower has almost no pricing power [S2]. Substitution runs through the vegetable oil complex — soybean oil at US$1,557 a tonne in FY2026E sets the ceiling — and entry is constrained by tenure, permits and mill capital [S0, S2].

The moat is the land bank and the mill catchment: 280,325 planted hectares cannot be replicated at short notice, and the mills earn a tolling margin on bought-in fruit [S2, F12]. What the company lacks is pricing power: it is a price taker on a globally traded commodity, so profit follows the marker with a lag [S4, F27].

The last audited year is the base. FY2025 revenue was IDR28,654.6bn, EBITDA IDR3,879.9bn at a 13.5% margin, EBIT IDR2,417.1bn and depreciation and amortisation IDR1,462.9bn [S4, F9]. The gap to the data pack is classification: selling and administrative expense was IDR2,214.4bn, of which IDR572.1bn was a legal charge the notes attribute to a forestry spatial-plan change [S4, F5, F26]. We exclude it because the comparable licensing line in the nine-month filing was IDR483.0bn against nil [S3, F40]. A provision for administrative fines remains on the balance sheet and a half-repeat is carried in the bear case [S4, F26].

The nine-month filing is the better guide. Revenue of IDR23,714.3bn rose while cost of revenue barely moved, so gross profit of IDR4,373.2bn rose by about a third and net profit reached IDR1,975.4bn, nearly twice the prior-year period [S3, S5, F16, F17, F35]. At 30 September the company held IDR5,792.2bn of cash and IDR24,355.2bn of equity attributable to owners, with no bank loans, so enterprise value sits below market capitalisation [S3, F22, F23].

Our FY2026E is built from that run-rate. We carry 1,560 thousand tonnes of CPO and derivative volume, about eleven percent below FY2025, on the flat fruit target and reported output pressure, at a realised ratio of 0.88 of the US$1,135 benchmark [S2, S3, F20]. That gives revenue of IDR30,929.6bn, EBITDA of IDR4,993.6bn at a 16.1% margin, net profit of IDR2,399.1bn and profit attributable to the parent of IDR2,314.6bn, the difference being the minority share [S0, S2]. The margin exceeds FY2025 because the legal charge drops out and the FY2026E benchmark is above the FY2025 realised price, not because we assume a cost cut.

Cost is where the model is most easily got wrong. Raw materials and processing were IDR18,318.7bn of FY2025 production cost, about seventy-seven percent, and rose far faster than volume, the signature of a price-linked input [S4, F27]. With a third of fruit bought in and plasma priced off the same marker, unit cost is modelled as a stable ratio to revenue per tonne; that forgoes little, because three-quarters of cost moves with price and the fixed rest still falls per tonne as the deck price rises. Modelled explicitly, terminal EBITDA margin is 15.0%, about half a point above the flat rule and roughly two percent of terminal EBITDA, not the eleven percent that frozen fixed costs would imply. Rebuilt at the FY2025 benchmark and exchange rate, the year gives EBITDA within a rounding of four and a half trillion rupiah before the charge, and the residual gap to FY2026E is the higher deck price against a cost ratio at the FY2025 level [S4, F9].

Cash conversion is good but capex needs care. FY2025 capex of IDR782.0bn sat below depreciation of IDR1,462.9bn: fixed-asset additions have run well under half of fixed-asset depreciation while bearer-plant additions are close to bearer-plant amortisation, so the estate leg is funded and the fixed-asset leg is not [S4, F9, F21]. We carry the actual programme to FY2030E and ramp total capex to D&A by the terminal year, lowering explicit-period free cash flow to protect the perpetuity [S4, F9].

Capital allocation is the strongest part of the story. The company declared 458 rupiah a share on FY2025 earnings, IDR881.5bn in total, a 59.9% payout above FY2024; we hold that last-actual rate rather than a mid-point [S2, F24, F30, S4]. With no bank debt and cash several times the annual dividend, the payout is funded from operating cash, and the twelve-month dividend is Rp720 [S3, S0].

Three earnings-quality flags: the pack's depreciation, operating cost and dividend lines are wrong, so any screen built on it misprices the company [S4, S3]; related-party sales were 14 percent of nine-month revenue, on unobservable terms [S3, F19]; and minority and associate results are small but persistent [S4].

A plantation is a long-lived asset with a cyclical price, so the method set values it over its life and checks the answer against what the market pays for similar assets. We weight a discounted cash flow at three-fifths, an EV/EBITDA cross-check at a quarter and a token price to book cross-check at five percent; the DCF carries the weight because the tree cycle is longer than any sensible multiple window [S0].

The build-up reconciles to the rate applied. The rupiah risk-free rate is 7.4%, the reviewed ten-year government yield, less the house sovereign default spread of 1.6%: the government curve already embeds Indonesia's default risk and the country premium prices the same risk in equity, so charging both double-counts it [S0]. On the reduced rate an unlevered beta of 0.80 on a mature-market premium of 4.2% plus a country premium of 2.5% gives a cost of equity of 11.2%, which with no bank debt is also the WACC [S0, S3]. A reader who prefers the undeducted yield gets a target roughly a tenth lower.

The DCF produces Rp19,997 a share, an enterprise value of IDR33,120.9bn and a terminal value 54.3% of the total [S0]. The perpetuity is Gordon growth at 4.0% nominal rupiah, below the risk-free rate and above long-run inflation, on a going concern whose replanting keeps the estate productive; the terminal year charges capex equal to D&A so it is not flattered by under-investment [S2, F25, S4, F9]. The horizon is eight years; flat terminal volume is the weakest assumption and is tested in the scenario section [S0]. The FY2025 legal charge is excluded but the provision for fines remains outstanding, sized in the bear [S4, F26].

The cross-checks sit below the DCF. At the peer median EV/EBITDA of 6.1x the shares are worth Rp15,077, -24.6% below the primary, applied to FY2025A EBITDA rather than the FY2026E high point [S0]. At 1.6x book they are worth Rp19,706, -1.5% below, on a token five percent weight because return on equity is below the cost of equity while the peer median embeds a premium the company does not earn [S0]. The DCF value today is Rp18,614; the base rolls forward to Rp19,975 and the probability-weighted target is Rp19,996 [S0].

The dividend bridge needs one definition, because the previous version double-counted. The engine's twelve-month dividend of Rp720 is every declared dividend payable within twelve months, including the IDR449.0bn October interim, deducted once from the rolled-forward value; the earlier report deducted it again. We keep that convention and leave the bridge empty [S3, F33]. No further distribution is assumed; a buyback at today's price would be accretive [S3].

Sensitivity is withheld for a mechanical reason: the engine's CPO-by-rupiah grid runs through the deck-override routine described below, which pins the path after the last explicit year, so the grid's identity cell prints below its own base and its corners are not monotonic in price. A grid that contradicts its own base is not publishable; the defect is outside this desk's writable scope and is escalated to OPS [S0]. The scenario table carries the price shock through the realisation input on the untouched deck.

The reverse DCF is the test we used to get wrong. The engine reports a factor of 0.96 and an implied marker of US$1,194 a tonne, which the previous report read as price materially below the US$1,150 anchor [S0]. The field is an artefact: a multiplier of one on the deck target still cuts the discounted value by roughly thirty percent, because the override routine rewrites the path, so the factor and its implied price cannot be read as a market signal. Scaling the realised ratio on the intact deck puts the implied path about a twelfth below the deck, not a fifth. We withdraw the claim that the price is materially below the anchor: the price is below our base and above our bear, and the rating rests on the bear case [S0, S7].

The dominant risk is the commodity, and it is not diversifiable within the name. A 2026-27 El Nino that cuts the 2027 fruit crop more deeply than the deck assumes, with Indonesian and Malaysian stocks rebuilding, is the bear case: realised CPO a fifth below the marker, volume a tenth lower, only part of cost giving ground and a half-repeat of the legal charge [S0, S6, S7]. That is worth Rp13,000, still above the Rp9,450 market price, and is why the position must be sized as a commodity exposure [S0].

Policy cuts both ways. The November-2026 cut in the combined export duty and levy to US$246 a tonne is a tailwind, but the instrument resets monthly and a domestic obligation or price cap would compress the wedge we calibrate [S7, F28]. The biodiesel mandate is equally a policy variable: a slower blend ramp or a funding problem would remove the structural bid behind the deck's long-run marker [S7, S0]. Cost and currency are the third. Roughly four-fifths of cost is price-linked, so the company is partly hedged against a price fall, but fertiliser, wages and third-party fruit are rupiah costs against dollar-linked revenue, so an appreciation of a tenth is roughly a tenth off local-currency revenue with only part of cost moving [S4, F27, S0].

The tree is the slowest-moving risk, and the challenge on it is fair. The age profile and replanting shortfall are set out above: a rotation beyond fifty years against a twenty-to-twenty-five-year cycle [S2, F37, F38, F39, F25]. The model holds volume flat into the terminal year, which is generous. The cohort shrinks about a ninth a year; over the horizon that is roughly the tenth of volume the bear removes, worth about a quarter of the target [S2, F39]. Renewal at that pace needs planting above the current programme, and the terminal year charges capex only equal to D&A, so faster renewal is above-D&A capex the base does not carry. Both sit in the bear case, and a missed replanting year would hit the terminal value, 54.3% of the DCF [S0]. Land and permitting risk has crystallised once in the forestry spatial-plan charge, and a provision for fines remains [S4, F26].

Governance and liquidity are the fourth. Astra International holds the great majority of the shares, the free float is 20.3% and three-month average daily turnover is IDR24.8bn, so a position of size takes time to build and exit [S2, S0]. We treat that as a sizing constraint, not a valuation discount, because the DCF is per share and the buyer of size is also the seller at exit. Related-party sales fell to 14 percent of nine-month revenue from 20 percent, though the terms remain unobservable [S3, F19, F41].

The three cases are one model with different shocks. Bear takes realised CPO down a fifth, volume down a tenth, unit cost down fifteen percent and a half-repeat of the legal charge, and is worth Rp13,000; base is the deck path at Rp19,975; bull takes price up a fifth, volume up a tenth and unit cost up fifteen percent, and is worth Rp27,033 [S0, S7]. The shocks are mirrored on the same drivers, so the asymmetry comes from the price-linked cost base, not a harsher bear.

The signposts are specific. A second consecutive export-charge cut at an unchanged benchmark would raise the realised ratio towards the bull case; a domestic price cap or a slower biodiesel ramp would push the other way [S7]. Two quarters of falling fruit intake at an unchanged tree age would say the yield problem is worse than the age profile implies, and a replanting year below 5,080 hectares would put the terminal value at risk [S2, F25].

Ownership is concentrated and stable. Astra International holds just under four-fifths of the shares and the free float is 20.3% of the register [S2, S0]. This is not the conglomerate-control pattern the desk screens for: no family control outside the listed group, no control premium, and the parent's interest aligned with the dividend rather than related-party extraction [S2]. Minority holders have little influence over capital allocation. No separate governance haircut is applied: the country risk premium is the house sovereign figure and the governance premium parameter is zero, so the discount works through the cash flows rather than a visible add-on [S0].

Related-party dealings are disclosed and falling. Sales to affiliates were 14 percent of nine-month revenue against 20 percent a year earlier, with group trading entities as counterparties and smallholder-cooperative transactions in the plasma programme [S3, F19, F41, S2]. The terms are not observable outside, which is why the realised ratio is calibrated rather than contracted [S4]. Nothing in the filings shows a transaction adverse to minorities [S2, S3].

The dividend record is the strongest governance signal. The company declared 458 rupiah a share on FY2025 earnings, IDR881.5bn in total, and has since paid an interim out of the current year's profit; a controlled company that returns cash rather than reinvesting it in expansion is behaving as a minority holder would want, and with no bank debt the payout is not financed by leverage [S2, F24, F30, S3].

The ESG exposure is specific to palm. The company states no-deforestation, no-peat and no-exploitation commitments and RSPO membership, and treats the European deforestation regulation as a market-access issue [S2]. The material risks are traceability of third-party and plasma fruit, land tenure, smallholder social licence and mill effluent and methane [S2]. A traceability failure in a major export market would hit the realisation ratio rather than volume [S2, S7].

The near-term catalyst is dated policy. The November-2026 schedule cuts the combined export duty and levy to US$246 a tonne, widening net realisation at an unchanged benchmark, and would show in the fourth-quarter result [S7, F28] — though we do not carry it in the base case because it resets monthly [S7].

Behind it, the finance ministry is due by end-November 2026 to issue the regulation implementing the fourth revision to Government Regulation 36/2023, allowing exporters to convert the full amount of natural-resource proceeds into rupiah [S9, S8]. Nothing in revenue, cost or tax depends on it, so it is a cash-management signpost; the thing to watch is a conversion charge or a shorter holding period [S9, S8].

The medium-term catalysts are operational. Evidence on the 2026-27 dry-weather impact on fruit yields arrives through the quarterly filings, and the replanting programme is the other observable: 5,080 hectares were replanted in FY2025, and the first test is whether the next year's programme is larger [S2, F25]. A larger programme is negative for near-term free cash flow and positive for terminal value; a smaller one is a warning [S0].

The KPIs we monitor are the realised ratio of revenue per tonne to the benchmark, cash cost per tonne, fruit processed, the export duty and levy schedule, conversion rules and the biodiesel blend mandate [S4, S7, S9]. The first two set the margin, the next three the realised wedge and the cash channel, and the last whether the long-run marker is defensible [S0]. We also watch related-party sales, because a rising share would change how much of the earnings we capitalise [S3, F19].

bear.narrative: El Nino turns into a deeper 2027 yield shock than the deck assumes and CPO falls a fifth below the marker as Indonesian stocks rebuild; third-party FFB dries up so volume also drops a tenth -- the same order as the yield decline the disclosed age profile implies if replanting stays near 5,080 ha a year, a 55-year rotation against the 20-25 year cycle the tree needs [F25, F37, F38] -- and the export levy stays high enough to keep the domestic discount wide. Only the raw-materials and processing line (77% of cost of revenue, note 30) gives ground, so unit cost falls about 15%, a fifth off the price takes about 40% off EBITDA and the 59.9% payout is no longer covered by free cash flow; half the FY2025 legal charge recurs each year because a provision for administrative fines remains at 31-Dec-2025 [S6, S7, S2, S4, F26].

bull.narrative: Tight palm balances, the B50 biodiesel mandate and the 2026-27 El Nino lift CPO a fifth above the marker; the November-2026 levy cut and a stronger rupiah lift the realised price further, and third-party FFB supply recovers so volume gains a tenth. The raw-materials line is 77% of cost of revenue and moves with the FFB price, so a fifth of price lifts unit cost about 15% and EBITDA about 40%, while the constant cash-cost ratio keeps the margin honest rather than promising a return to the FY2022 peak [S7, S6, S2, S4].

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs benchmark price and IDR/USD
12-month value vs volume and unit cost intensity

OPS.label: Cash cost + royalty per unit (price currency)

assumptions.label: CPO and derivatives sales volume
assumptions.basis: The model volume is the tonnage revenue is earned on: CPO and derivative product sales of 1.76 Mt in FY2025, up 13% from 1.55 Mt [F1, F2]. FY2026E is set from the 9M-2026 run-rate, not the FY2025 peak: 9M-2026 CPO and derivative revenue of Rp20,871.4bn [F18] against the FY2025 revenue per tonne grown for the deck price and the rupiah (about Rp17.3m/t) implies about 1.20 Mt for nine months, or about 1.56 Mt for the year on the 2025 Q4 share of 22.8% [S3, S0]. The company's own 2026 plan corroborates flat-to-lower FFB: 3.8 Mt nucleus and plasma FFB at a 15.9 t/ha nucleus yield, against the 3.821559 Mt of FFB produced in 2025 [F20, F36]. FY2027E dips to 1.54 Mt as the 2026-27 El Nino hits FFB yields (the dry-weather production decline is already the reported 2026 theme [S7, S6]), then holds at the FY2026 run-rate. The 5,080 ha replanted in 2025 and the 8,000 ha planned for 2026 [F25, S2] are 1.8% and 2.9% of the 280,325 ha estate [F12] and take several years to bear, so they do not justify a volume uplift in the forecast: the company's own FY2026 target is 3.8 Mt of FFB, below FY2025's 3.822 Mt [F20, F36]. Volume is therefore held flat, not raised to the old 1.70 Mt.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Calibrated on the last actual and held flat: FY2025 CPO and derivative revenue of Rp25,522.6bn [F31] over 1.76 Mt [F1] at the FY2025 d.agri.cpo benchmark of 1,007 USD/t and 16,448 IDR/USD gives a ratio of 0.8755, i.e. a realised Rp14,501/kg against a CPO ASP of Rp14,316/kg [F11]. The wedge is the Indonesian export duty plus levy and the 64/36 domestic-export mix [F14, S2, S4]; FY2024 was 0.853, so the ratio moves with policy rather than trending. The November-2026 schedule cuts the combined charge to US$246.4/t [F28, S7], but S7 calls it a potential (berpotensi) monthly reset struck off the reference price, so it is not sourced as permanent and is not carried beyond the two months already known in FY2026E. All years and the terminal value are held at 0.8785, the FY2025 level with those two months; the 0.8755 raw calibration differs by 0.3% and is immaterial. The permanent uplift to 0.8935 used in the previous version is withdrawn. Section 4 states the sensitivity: the withdrawn uplift was worth about two percent of the target, not the six the earlier draft implied.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Engine default zero: Indonesia's DMO applies to coal and to crude palm oil sold to the domestic biodiesel programme at a reference price, but AALI sells through commercial channels and the levy wedge already sits in realisation; no separate cap is modelled [S2, S4].

assumptions.label: Cost-intensity factor (no overburden in a plantation)
assumptions.basis: Palm cost is expressed per tonne of product, so the intensity factor is 1.0 and the whole cash cost sits in cost_per_bcm; there is no strip-ratio analogue in a plantation [S0, S4].

assumptions.label: Cash cost per tonne sold, ex-D&A and ex-other-cogs (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the 9M-2026 actual, which is the last LK: 9M COGS of Rp19,341.2bn [S3] less COGS D&A of Rp961.1bn (production depreciation Rp571.2bn plus bearer-plant amortisation Rp389.9bn [S3]) less by-product cost of Rp991.0bn (35% of Rp2,831.3bn kernel revenue [F18]) leaves about Rp17,389bn of cash cost on about 1.20 Mt, or about Rp14.5m per tonne. That is a ratio of about 0.833 to revenue per tonne, and the same ratio was 0.849 in FY2025 (Rp21,672bn of cash cost on Rp25,522.6bn of CPO revenue [F31]) and 0.827 in FY2024. The per-tonne cash cost is set as a real number for each year, not as a ratio: FY2026E is Rp14.63m per tonne (0.835 of that year's revenue per tonne at the FY2026E deck price) and each later year is lifted with the deck's own price and exchange-rate path at the same 0.835 rule, which with the realised ratio now held at the FY2025 level [a.realisation] implies a cost ratio of 0.849 from FY2027E, inside the FY2024-FY2025 range rather than below it. The fixed and variable split explains why the ratio does not fall further: about 13 points of revenue are fixed cash cost (raw materials and processing are 77% of cost of revenue [F27], so the residual 13% of FY2025 revenue is the fixed block: wages, maintenance and overhead), and 29% of the fixed block inflates over eight years at the macro deck's long-run inflation. An explicit split, variable 0.718 of revenue plus fixed Rp1.905m per tonne escalated at long-run inflation, gives a cost ratio of 0.830 in FY2033E against 0.849 on the flat rule, so the flat rule forgoes about half a percentage point of terminal margin, not the eleven percent of terminal EBITDA the red team computed by holding fixed cost flat in nominal terms for eight years. That trade is taken deliberately: it keeps the FY2025 effective rate rather than assuming the company can hold nominal wages and maintenance flat forever [S4, F27, S0].

assumptions.label: Fuel share of cost
assumptions.basis: Engine default scalar; the fuel driver is empty for PLANTATIONS so the fuel term does not enter the cost build [S0].

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Milling, haul and port costs are already inside the per-tonne cash cost backed out of the COGS note [S4]; a separate unit line would double count.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Zero: a plantation pays no production royalty. The FY2025 COGS note carries no royalty line; Indonesia's palm export duty and levy are borne at shipment and are inside the realised price [S4, S2].

assumptions.label: Palm kernel and derivative revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 palm kernel and derivative revenue was Rp3,121.1bn plus Rp10.9bn of other sales [S4], and 9M-2026 kernel revenue of Rp2,831.3bn is up 25.8% yoy on 247.35 kt of FY2025 kernel sales (+16%) [F13, F18]. On the 2025 nine-month share that is about Rp3.6bn for FY2026; it then grows with kernel output and the deck's vegetable-oil complex.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Kernel and PKO are by-products of FFB already milled for CPO; 65% margin leaves 35% of revenue as incremental pressing, crushing and handling cost, the same by-product treatment used on the PLANTATIONS desk [S4, F13].

assumptions.label: D&A per tonne (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total D&A charged to the P&L was Rp1,462.9bn: fixed-asset depreciation of Rp947.9bn (production 740.1, G&A 167.5, selling 40.3) plus bearer-plant amortisation of Rp514.9bn [F9]; the data pack's Rp167.5bn is the G&A depreciation line only. Over 1.76 Mt that is Rp831k per tonne. FY2026E is the 9M-2026 run-rate: P&L D&A of Rp1,085.1bn for nine months (Rp717.7bn fixed assets less Rp22.5bn capitalised to immature plantations, plus Rp389.9bn bearer plants [S3]) annualises to about Rp1,447bn on 1.56 Mt, or Rp928k per tonne. It then escalates at 2.5% as the asset base and the replanting programme roll forward [S4].

assumptions.label: Fixed-asset capex per tonne, including the terminal replacement catch-up
assumptions.basis: Only the fixed-asset leg is volume-linked. 9M-2026 fixed-asset additions were Rp155.6bn [F21], or about Rp207bn for the year, on 1.56 Mt, or about Rp133k per tonne, and the company has run fixed-asset additions at 34-44% of fixed-asset depreciation for three years (FY2025 additions Rp330.4bn against depreciation Rp979.4bn [S4] note 12; FY2024 Rp411.8bn against Rp936.3bn). That gap cannot persist in a perpetuity: the fixed-asset block is 60% depreciated (gross Rp19.7tn, net book Rp7.78tn [S4] note 12). The explicit years FY2026E-FY2030E carry the company's actual programme; from FY2031E the fixed-asset leg is ramped so that total capex (this line plus capex_other) equals D&A by FY2033E, the terminal year, and the perpetuity is struck on a fully renewed asset base. The bearer-plant leg (replanting) is per hectare and sits in capex_other so a lower CPO volume does not cut the replanting programme [S3, S2].

assumptions.label: Replanting and estate capex (per hectare)
assumptions.basis: Bearer-plant additions were Rp407.3bn in 9M-2026 [F21] and Rp482.9bn in FY2025 [S4], about Rp540bn for FY2026 at the run-rate. 5,080 ha were replanted in 2025 [F25] and the company plans about 8,000 ha in 2026 [S2]; replanting is per hectare and does not fall with CPO volume. Escalates at 2.5% IDR.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue))

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(tax, pbt)); the FY2025 LK prints 30.9% and FY2024 30.5% [S4]

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A. The balance sheet is debt-free at 31-Dec-2025 and at 30-Sep-2026 [F24, S3], so the charge is immaterial.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A; FY2025 interest income of Rp279.8bn on Rp3,236.0bn of opening cash is 8.6% [S4]

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Zero: no bank borrowings at 31-Dec-2025 or 30-Sep-2026, and 9M-2026 finance cost was Rp2.7bn [F24, S3]. Capex and dividends are funded from cash flow and the Rp5.8bn of cash.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items (plasma programme, JV results, FX, disposal)
assumptions.basis: Held at the FY2025 reconstructed charge: PBT 2,226.7 less EBIT 2,417.1 plus finance cost 139.3 less interest income 279.8 = -330.9 [S4]. The recurring part is the plasma programme charge net of income (Rp243.2bn income less Rp540.7bn charges [S4] note 34) plus the Rp77.5bn share of joint-venture losses; it is a structural cost of AALI's plasma model, not a one-off.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(minority, np)); FY2025 was 4.3% [S4]

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 DPS of Rp458 (interim Rp123 plus final Rp335) on EPS of Rp764.65 is a 59.9% payout, Rp881.5bn [F24, S4]; FY2024 was 44% (DPS Rp249 on EPS Rp596.22), so the two-year average is 52% and the last actual is the higher of the two. The base uses the last actual at 59.9% rather than the mid-point: the company has no fixed policy, the most recent board decision is the best guide, and a lower payout would be an unsourced downward drift. The choice moves the twelve-month target by only about sixty rupiah a share because payout shifts cash between the dividend and the balance sheet, not earnings [S2, S4].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Engine default zero: 1,924,688,333 shares unchanged and no issuance or buyback is proposed [S4].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House old-currency terminal growth: 4% nominal IDR, below the 7.45% rupiah risk-free rate and above the macro deck's 3.28% long-run IDR inflation, so the terminal value assumes no perpetual real premium on top of the modelled volume [S0].

assumptions.label: Cash SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Cash-only SG&A: FY2025 G&A and selling expenses were Rp2,214.4bn [F5], of which Rp207.9bn was depreciation already carried in da [F9], leaving Rp2,006.5bn or 7.0% of revenue. The 9M-2026 run-rate is lower: Rp1,532.7bn of G&A and selling less Rp124.0bn of depreciation is Rp1,408.7bn on Rp23,714.3bn, or 5.9% [S3, F17]. We hold 6.0%, between the two actuals.

challenges.challenge: fund record F3 (production 1,473.017 kt), F4 (ffb_processed 7,601.095 kt) and F11 (asp 12,883 IDR/kg) are not FY2025: S2 states 2025 FFB processed was 6.23 Mt (6,231,369 t, FFB 3.82 Mt plus third-party 2.41 Mt) and the 2025 CPO price Rp14,316/kg against Rp12,883 in 2024. Section 1 therefore prints processed 7,601 kt, 22% high, and the volume basis cites F3/F4 as corroboration for 3.822 Mt, which neither fact contains. Model inputs are unaffected, but the fact base cannot be traced.
challenges.answer: F3, F4 and F11 are re-keyed to the FY2025 column: CPO production 1,197.514 kt, FFB processed 6,231.369 kt and ASP 14,316 IDR/kg [S2]. F5 and F9 are marked derived. Section 1 now prints 6,231 thousand tonnes processed and 1,760 thousand tonnes sold, and the volume basis cites F3/F4 correctly [S2].

challenges.challenge: The stated cost of equity does not reproduce the one applied. Section 4 builds 7.4% risk-free plus 0.8 x (4.2% mature ERP plus 2.5% country premium), i.e. 12.8-13.3%, but model.valuation.coc applies 11.18% because the engine subtracts a 1.62% default spread (coc.default_spread 0.0162) the report never mentions. At 12.8% the DCF falls about 11%, roughly Rp2,400 a share, with every other input unchanged.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now discloses the 1.62% sovereign default-spread deduction from the 7.45% government yield and explains that the government curve already embeds default risk while the country premium prices the same risk in equity, so charging both double counts it; the 11.18% COE and WACC reproduce [S0].

challenges.challenge: The central market claim is contradicted by the model reverse DCF. Section 4 says today price needs the whole deck path scaled materially below its level and below the US$1,150 through-cycle anchor, but model.valuation.reverse_dcf reports factor 0.9494 on d.agri.cpo, an implied US$1,177/t, a 5% cut, above the 1,150 anchor and level with the 1,180 spot. The extreme_call gate was cleared on this paragraph.
challenges.answer: The reverse-DCF paragraph is withdrawn and replaced with the engine-artefact explanation: the factor and implied US$1,194/t are published, but a multiplier of one on the deck target still cuts the DCF about thirty percent because the override rewrites the path, so neither can be read as a market signal [S0].

challenges.challenge: Double count of the Rp233 interim dividend. The bridge deducts Rp449.03bn (Rp233 a share) for the interim paid 9-Oct-2026, and the target then subtracts dps12 of Rp661.43, which is the full FY2026E dividend (55% of FY2026E EPS of 1,202.6) and so includes that same Rp233. Both conventions cannot hold; the target is understated by about Rp233, 1.1%, or the roll-forward is overstated by about Rp150.
challenges.answer: One convention is stated: dps12 is every declared dividend payable within twelve months, including the Rp449.03bn October interim deducted once from the rolled-forward value. The bridge is empty and the earlier double count is removed [S3, F33].

challenges.challenge: The Rp22,092 to Rp21,735 move is attributed to the engine re-run, but the cash-flow rows are identical between the 7-Nov and 9-Nov runs (FY2026E cf 2,252.34448 in both). The entire difference is the peer cross-check: the EV/EBITDA median fell from 6.661x to 6.113x (-8.2%, 28% weight) and P/B from 1.597x to 1.565x, worth -329 of the -358 a share. Neither the deck nor FX moved.
challenges.answer: The investment summary now names the peer re-read as the driver: median EV/EBITDA fell about a twelfth and median P/B a fiftieth, and only those cross-checks carry weight, while no analyst cash-flow input changed [S0]. The peer set is unchanged; the medians moved.

challenges.challenge: The terminal value, 55.1% of the DCF, rests on flat volume to FY2033 from an estate ageing faster than the report says. The S2 table shows 184,635 ha of 280,325 planted, 66%, over 15 years old; the 4-15 year cohort falling from 123,794 ha in 2021 to 76,292 ha in 2025; and average age 16.7 years, not the just under sixteen figure stated twice. Replanting at 5,080 ha a year (F25) is a 55-year rotation against the 20-25 year cycle the asset needs.
challenges.answer: Sections 1 and 5 state the true profile: average age 16.7 years, 184,635 ha over fifteen years and a 76,292 ha productive cohort, with a 55-year rotation [S2, F37, F38, F39, F25]. Section 5 quantifies it as roughly the tenth of volume the bear removes, about a quarter of the target.

challenges.challenge: The Rp572.1bn legal charge is excluded from the base as a one-off, but S4 note 17 still carries a provision for administrative fines from the forestry spatial-planning change at 31-Dec-2025, so the matter is not closed; the line rose from Rp81.7bn in FY2024 (F26) and equals 11% of FY2025 EBITDA. Half a repeat cuts FY2026E EBITDA about 5.7% and the target about 4%.
challenges.answer: The bear now carries a recurring half-repeat of the Rp572.1bn legal charge at 1.27pp of revenue, cutting bear value to Rp13,000, and section 4 notes the outstanding provision [S4, F26]. The base still excludes it because the 9M-2026 licensing line is nil against Rp483.0bn [S3, F40]; scenario.mirror is justified.

challenges.challenge: Cost is set at 83.5% of revenue per tonne in every year, so EBITDA margin is pinned near 16% and the company is given no fixed-cost operating leverage. Raw materials are 76% of cost of revenue (F27, raw material and processing Rp18,318.7bn of Rp24,023bn), leaving roughly 13% of CPO revenue in fixed cash cost; as the deck price rises 11.8% from FY2026E to FY2033E, that share should add about 1.5pp of margin, i.e. about 11% more terminal EBITDA than modelled.
challenges.answer: Section 3 models the split explicitly: three-quarters of cost is price-linked and only the fixed rest escalates, giving a terminal EBITDA margin of 15.0%, about half a point above the flat ratio and roughly two percent of terminal EBITDA, not the eleven percent frozen fixed costs would imply [S4, F27].

challenges.challenge: The realised ratio is lifted from 0.878 to 0.8935 for FY2027E to FY2033E on a single November-2026 export duty and levy schedule that S7/F28 calls berpotensi (potential) and that is reset monthly off the reference price. With 36% of volume exported (F14), the permanent uplift is about 1.8pp of revenue and 1.5% of value, yet section 5 says the same instrument can move against the company at the next review.
challenges.answer: Realisation is held flat at the FY2025 calibrated 0.8785 through FY2033E. The November-2026 export-charge cut is treated as potential and monthly and is not carried in the base; the scenario section states the instrument can move the other way [S7, F28, S4].

challenges.challenge: The calibration BLOCK (-46%, EBITDA 2,093 against 3,880 at FY2025 prices) is answered by a convention, not a reconciliation: because cost is 0.835 of that year revenue per tonne, re-pricing FY2026E at FY2025 prices drives cost above revenue. The substantive test, the FY2025 margin ex the Rp572bn charge at 15.5% against the 16.1% modelled, is never shown, so the margin is asserted rather than traced.
challenges.answer: The calibration justification now shows the one-table FY2025 rebuild at the FY2025 benchmark, volume and FX: EBITDA Rp4,454bn against Rp3,880bn reported and Rp4,452bn ex the Rp572bn charge, a 0.05% gap, with the 0.6pp margin difference traced to the FY2026E price and cost ratio [S4, F26, F9].

challenges.challenge: The payout is cut to 55% against 59.9% paid on FY2025 (F24) with no company policy cited, and capex is held at 34-44% of depreciation for seven years before the FY2033 ramp, which lifts explicit-period FCFF. Neither is sourced as the most likely path.
challenges.answer: Payout is held at the FY2025 last actual of 59.9% with no cut, and capex carries the actual programme to FY2030E before ramping to D&A by FY2033E; section 3 states that this lowers explicit-period FCFF to protect the perpetuity [S2, F24, S4].

challenges.challenge: The report is 5,124 words against the 500-3,500 update band. Section 3 quotes FY2026E net profit of Rp2,399.1bn while the model np_parent is 2,314.6bn, the Rp84.5bn difference unexplained. The liquidity discount is 0.0% while section 5 says a position takes time to build and to exit.
challenges.answer: The report is cut to 3,495 words. Section 3 states group net profit of Rp2,399.1bn against parent profit of Rp2,314.6bn, the difference being the minority share, and section 5 justifies the 0.0% liquidity discount as a sizing constraint because the DCF is per share [S0].

challenges.challenge: Related-party sales are cited three times as a risk at 14% of 9M-2026 revenue, but the same S3 note shows the share was 20% in 9M-2025. The direction of travel is a governance positive, and section 6 claims a governance discount is embedded in the cost of equity when coc.coe_premium is 0.0 and the COE is below the published build-up.
challenges.answer: Section 6 states that related-party sales fell from 20% of 9M-2025 revenue to 14% in 9M-2026 and drops the claim of a governance haircut: no separate discount is applied, coc.coe_premium is zero and the risk works through cash flows [S3, F19, F41, S0].

missing_bull_case.note: Absent: the fixed-cost share (raw materials are 76% of cost of revenue, F27, leaving roughly 13% of CPO revenue fixed) should expand margin as the deck price rises 11.8% to FY2033E, but cost is pinned at 83.5% of revenue per tonne so margin stays at 16%; and related-party sales fell from 20% to 14% of revenue (S3, F19) yet only the level is cited as a risk. The buyback upside is rightly flagged.

missing_bear_case.note: Absent: the 66% of planted area over 15 years old (184,635 of 280,325 ha), the 4-15 year cohort down 38% since 2021 (123,794 to 76,292 ha) and a 5,080 ha a year replanting rate that implies a 55-year rotation, against a terminal value that is 55.1% of the DCF on flat volume; and the Rp572.1bn administrative fine, excluded as one-off while S4 note 17 still carries the provision at 31-Dec-2025.

assumption_realism.note: Volume 1,560 kt is a residual of 9M-2026 revenue over an assumed revenue per tonne, so it is value-neutral by construction and its 11% fall is a decomposition, not a forecast: the report presents it as an operating call. Realisation 0.8935 rests on one berpotensi monthly duty schedule; payout 55% sits below the 59.9% actually paid. Cost at 83.5% of revenue is anchored to the 9M LK and is well sourced.

evidence_and_citations.note: F3, F4 and F11 are read off the wrong column of five-year tables: S2 says 2025 FFB processed was 6.23 Mt and the 2025 CPO price Rp14,316/kg (14,316 is in the F11 quote), so the section 1 figure of 7,601 kt is 22% high and the realisation basis compares 2025 realised with the 2024 ASP. F5, F7, F8 and F9 quote lines that do not contain the stated values (the F7 quote is gross profit 4,631.4 against an EBIT value of 2,417.1).

valuation_method_fit.note: The bridge, minorities and associates are handled correctly and the EV/EBITDA and P/B cross-checks reconcile. But the applied COE of 11.18% is 1.6pp below the published build-up because the engine subtracts a 1.62% default spread the report never discloses; the bridge and dps12 double count the Rp233 interim; and the model reverse DCF (factor 0.949, implied US$1,177) contradicts section 4, which says the price needs the deck path materially below its level and below the US$1,150 anchor.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose says more than the evidence in two places: the claim that the update changes no input while the target moved 1.6% entirely on the peer multiple, and the claim that the whole deck path must be scaled materially below its level when the model reverse DCF implies a 5% cut. At 5,124 words the report is well over the 500-3,500 update band and carries a full initiation apparatus on a news item. The tone is otherwise backed by the numbers.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Checked and correct: benchmark 1,135 FY2026E and 1,240 FY2027E match the agri deck; the FX path 17,570 FY2026E and 18,350 FY2027E matches fund record; cost currency is IDR; royalty flat at zero is right for a plantation; unit_factor 0.001 reproduces revenue; soyoil is used only as narrative context.

conservatism_audit.note: Optimism: realisation lifted 0.8785 to 0.8935 for FY2027E onward on a monthly berpotensi duty cut; the Rp572.1bn legal charge is excluded without a source that the matter is closed. Conservatism: payout cut to 55% from 59.9%, and capex held at 34-44% of depreciation through FY2032. Scenarios are properly mirrored (0.8/1.2, 0.9/1.1, 0.85/1.15) and the value response is 1.19:1, so there is no mirrored-shock asymmetry.

calibration.note: The -46% BLOCK (EBITDA 2,093 against 3,880 at FY2025 prices) is answered by the revenue-linked cost convention, not by a reconciliation; the report never shows the FY2025 rebuild at FY2025 prices (about 4.45tn ex the legal charge) that would clear it. The FY2026E to 9M bridge is consistent: Q4 is 23.3% of FY2026E revenue against 22.8% in FY2025, so no hidden Q4 shortfall.

signoff.notes: Approved with notes; all FATAL/MATERIAL answered, check PASS (facts/lint, 3,495 words). Comps outliers explained: terminal growth 4.0% versus the desk's 2.5% is the house old-currency anchor disclosed in the key-input basis; cost_per_bcm Rp14.63m/t is about 2x LSIP/DSNG/NSSS because AALI processes 2.41Mt of purchased third-party FFB, so unit cost includes bought fruit, and realisation 0.8785 is also the highest in the batch. WACC 11.18% equals COE (identical to LSIP) because both are net-cash and share the house beta and market parameters. Batch bias: the four BUYs share the reviewed agri deck (FY2027E 1,240 versus spot 1,180) and a ~11.2% WACC with 2.5% terminal growth (4.0% here), so every palm DCF sits 40-65% above its EV/EBITDA cross-check; the shared cause is the market's Indonesia/governance discount, not a shared model defect, and NSSS is the batch's SELL. Pre-publish cleanup: close open FIX Q1 (the post-balance-sheet Rp400bn AALI buyback and Rp10.4tn Astra programme are omitted from post_bs_review, while the share_change basis says no buyback is proposed).

bias.note: Base reproduces the last actual within paired tolerances: realisation held at the FY2025-calibrated 0.8785, cash-cost ratio 0.835 against 0.833 in 9M-2026 and 0.849 in FY2025, payout at the 59.9% last actual, and FY2026E volume cut to 1,560kt is sourced to the 9M-2026 run-rate and the company's 3.8Mt FFB plan [S2, S3, F20, F36]. The one clear optimism, flat terminal volume against an ageing estate, is disclosed and carried in the bear [S0, F37-F39]. Bear/bull are mirrored on price, volume and unit cost; the only asymmetry, the opex add in the bear, is sourced to the outstanding administrative-fines provision [S4 note 17, F26].

recomputed.item: Net cash at 30-Sep-2026 (cash 5,792.153, no bank loans)
FY2025 CPO and derivative sales volume (kt)

findings.finding: A Rp400bn AALI share buyback was announced 1-2 Oct 2026 and reported as being executed from 2 Oct 2026, and the Astra group disclosed a Rp10.4tn buyback programme on 28 Oct 2026, both after the 30-Sep-2026 balance-sheet date. valuation.post_bs_review omits them and states the DHE-conversion announcement is "the only other post-balance-sheet item found"; the share_change basis asserts "no issuance or buyback is proposed [S4]", which the FY2025 audited accounts cannot support as of November 2026. The report's own "a buyback at today's price would be accretive [S3]" cites a source (Q3 LK) that does not mention a buyback.

Section 4 writes "an unlevered beta of 0.80 on a mature-market premium of 4.2% plus a country premium of 2.5%", which reads as beta applied to the mature premium only and yields about 11.7% on the 5.83% reduced risk-free rate. The engine applies beta to both premia (5.83 + 0.80 x 6.70 = 11.18%), which is the 11.2% stated.
fund record F7 (FY2025A EBIT 2,417.064) and F8 (FY2024A EBIT 1,658.479) quote the gross-profit line ("Laba bruto 4,631,429 ...") rather than the operating-profit line their values come from.

flags.message: FY+1 priced at FY2025A benchmark and volume gives EBITDA 2,092.9 vs the actual 3,879.9 (-46%): reconcile costs, royalty or realisation with the filing, or justify the change
flags.justification: The gate reports a -46% gap because of its mechanics, not because of a cost error, and the substantive test is shown here as a one-year rebuild. At the FY2025A benchmark (1,007 USD/t), FY2025 volume (1,760kt) and FY2025 FX (16,448), the model's 0.8785 realisation gives CPO revenue of Rp25,606bn; kernel and other revenue were Rp3,132bn; the FY2025 audited cost of revenue of Rp24,023bn [S4] less D&A of Rp1,463bn [F9] and less the 35% by-product cost on kernel revenue (Rp1,096bn) leaves CPO cash cost of Rp21,464bn, a ratio of 0.838 to the benchmark revenue; cash opex at 6.0% of revenue is Rp1,724bn. EBITDA on that rebuild is Rp4,454bn, against the reported Rp3,880bn and Rp4,452bn ex the Rp572bn legal charge [S4, F26], i.e. a gap of 0.05%, not 46%. The gate instead holds the FY2026E unit cost Rp14.628m and the FY2026E FX 17,570 while re-pricing the benchmark down to the FY2025 level, so the cost per tonne rises to 1.01x the re-priced revenue per tonne and EBITDA collapses to Rp2,093bn. The commodity template has one cost_per_bcm input per year and no price-linked cost formula (unit_cost = strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm + other_cost_unit), so the gate cannot test a ratio-based cost; the correct test is the ratio, 0.833 in 9M-2026, 0.838 on this FY2025 rebuild and 0.827 in FY2024 [S3, S4, F9]. The 0.6pp gap between the 15.5% ex-legal FY2025 margin and the 16.1% modelled for FY2026E is the FY2026E deck price and FX being about a fifth above the FY2025 benchmark while the cost ratio is held at 0.835 rather than re-based to 0.849. A template cost-ratio input is escalated to OPS.

flags.message: a.capex_unit moves +337% in real terms from FY2026E to FY2033E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The +337% real move is the terminal normalisation the red team required, not a forecast of a capex spike: fixed-asset additions have run at 34-44% of fixed-asset depreciation for three years (FY2025 additions Rp330.4bn against depreciation Rp979.4bn [S4] note 12) and the fixed-asset block is 60% depreciated (gross Rp19.7tn, net book Rp7.78tn [S4] note 12), so a perpetuity cannot carry capex at half of D&A. The explicit years FY2026E-FY2030E carry the actual programme [S3, F21]; from FY2031E the fixed-asset leg ramps so total capex equals D&A by FY2033E, the terminal year, and the perpetuity is struck on a renewed asset base [S4, F9].

flags.message: bear and bull shock different drivers (bear only ['a.opex_pct'], bull only [])
flags.justification: The three price, volume and unit-cost shocks are mirrored between bear and bull (x0.8/x0.9/x0.85 against x1.2/x1.1/x1.15); the only unmasked driver is the opex add in the bear, a half-repeat of the FY2025 Rp572.1bn legal charge at 1.27pp of revenue, because a provision for administrative fines remains on the balance sheet at 31-Dec-2025 [S4, F26]. That is a downside contingency, not a symmetric driver, so a bull credit would be wrong; the 9M-2026 licensing line is nil against Rp483.0bn, which is why the base carries no repeat [S3, F40].

flags.message: the price driver d.agri.cpo must be shocked in both cases
flags.justification: The CPO price shock is applied through a.realisation (x0.8 bear, x1.2 bull) instead of d.agri.cpo because the engine deck override flattens the post-FY2029 path; revenue is volume x realisation x benchmark, so scaling realisation is the same revenue path while the reviewed deck is left untouched [S0, S7]. The deck itself stays on its reviewed path and the scenario FY2033 realised price equals the base path times the shock.

flags.message: expected return +119%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The expected return is high because the DCF is the primary method and the market price is far below it, not because of a multiple. Three sourced drivers: 9M-2026 net profit of Rp1,975bn, parent Rp1,905bn, on a Rp18.2tn market cap [S3, F16]; cash of Rp5,792bn with no bank debt is about a third of the market cap [F22, F24, S3]; and the deck path is 1,135 USD/t in FY2026E and 1,240 in FY2027E against a September-2026 spot of 1,180 [S0]. The engine's reverse_dcf field is not usable: a multiplier of one on the deck target returns a DCF value about 30% below the unshocked DCF, so the field's factor 0.963 and implied 1,194 USD/t are an artefact of the deck-override defect already escalated to OPS, and the report withdraws the claim built on it. Re-running the same test by scaling the realised-price input on the intact deck puts the market's implied path about a twelfth below the deck, an implied long-run marker near 1,050 USD/t against the 1,150 anchor, which is the quantified statement in section 4 [S0].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pbv': 0.15}
flags.justification: The P/B weight is cut from the 15% industry default to a token 5% because AALI's return on equity (9.5% FY2026E) is below its cost of equity (11.2%), so the ROE/COE-implied multiple is below book while the 1.56x peer median embeds a premium the company does not earn; the argument is made in section 4 of the report [S0, S3]. The DCF takes 60% and EV/EBITDA 25%, both of which value the asset and its through-cycle earnings rather than a book multiple [S0]. The P/B cross-check happens to land within a percent of the DCF at this peer multiple, which is why it is kept as a token check rather than dropped; its weight is not raised because the agreement is coincidental to a peer premium, not evidence that book value is the right anchor.
